verdicts.rewritten_summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

CAIRO 52 Jordan country profile: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: OutRight International Jordan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — Jordan abolished the colonial-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018.

verdicts.note: subject: this record (civic-space context for expression)
verdicts.rewritten_summary: HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance — the environment shaping online expression for visitors and locals alike.

CAIRO 52 analysis of Case No. 2092/2014 (Jordan): Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff (born 1977) sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

HRW (6 Jun 2024): in Egypt, Jordan and Kuwait, same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in some, yet authorities 'legally' harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws — alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation, so decriminalisation on paper does not equal safety.

Official translation of Japan's SOGI-promotion Act (Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity): defines 'gender identity', requires the government to publish annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity, and sets out the national basic plan — the statutory framework now governing official态度 to LGBT issues.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: HRW (18 Jul 2023): Japan's Supreme Court ruled the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work — she challenged the denial in 2015; a Tokyo district court had ruled for her in 2019 on her 'important legal interest' to live by her self-identified gender and awarded damages.

Kyodo News FOCUS (21 Jun 2023): Japan enacted its LGBT-understanding-promotion law after months of debate but the text was watered down amid a culture-war debate over transgender issues — documents the political contestation behind the statute.

Japan Cheapo inclusive-onsen guide: bathhouses (onsen, sento, super-sento) can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors; provides LGBTQ+-friendly venue recommendations, private-bath and co-ed-pool options, and practical etiquette — a direct visitor-utility page for gender-diverse travelers.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Freely AU first-person guide 'Using onsen in Japan as a trans person' (published 29 Mar 2023, last updated 10 Jul 2026): what to expect using bathhouses as a trans traveller — practical expectations, venue norms and transition-related concerns from lived experience.

Japan Gay Guide visitor outlook: most travelers experience little direct hostility or discrimination, especially in major tourist destinations; LGBTQ visibility is low, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags other developed countries — the standard visitor-risk posture for Japan.

Chambers Global Practice Guide update (Japan LGBTQ status): significant progress including enactment of the SOGI-promotion law, two pro-transgender Supreme Court decisions and one gay-friendly Supreme Court decision, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent — legal-status update useful for framing institutional protection.

CEDAW NGO shadow report on LBT persons in Japan (May 2009): situation characterised by invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation; lesbians, bisexual women and transgender persons face discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention — dated baseline for institutional-protection claims.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Kyrgyzstan): anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from MPs; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); ECOM data shows high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement.

TGEU Trans Rights Index Map 2024: Kyrgyzstan (2021) joined Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia in removing the right to legal gender recognition; for Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

University of Hawai'i at Manoa research guide 'Gender Identity and Sexual Identity in the Pacific and Hawai'i': resources on sexual and gender diversity across the Pacific, documenting identity expressions defined as homosexual/transgender only in Western vocabulary — including the Pinapinaaine/Binabinaaine role of Tuvalu and Kiribati (Besnier 2014, 'Gender on the edge', p. 327).
